name: Melanau Daro / Melanau Matu / Melanau Rajang
confidence_why: No description of Daro, Matu or Rajang (Belawai) Melanau says anything about stress (Norfazila 2026, Norfazila & Wan Robiah 2023 and Kawi & Dayang Sariah 2018 are silent, as is Rensch 2012), and the nearest statements for other Melanau lects pull opposite ways, Clayre 1972 putting citation-form stress on the final syllable in Dalat while Blust 2018 gives Malay-like penultimate stress across the chain, so any value for this variety would be a guess.

catalog_quote: Clayre 1972 p.50: '2.23 Supra[se]gmental Phonemes are predictable at the level of the phonological word. Spoken in isolation, a word has primary stress on the final syllable nucleus, accompanied by a rise in pitch which falls off from a peak to approximately the starting datum level. Polysyllabic words have a secondary stress, accompanied by a less marked pitch change, on the penultimate syllable nucleus.' p.51 fn.1: 'This general rule is perturbed when the penultimate vowel is /a/, before a final /a/. Then both the last two syllables have approximately equal stress'. p.57: 'In each word, the final vocoid is stressed. This rule holds even for words cognate with Malay, in which the stress is differently distributed in the word, as eg: [ka'in] /kain/ 'cloth', cf: ['kain] (Malay)'. p.84: 'this obscures the pronunciation rule which places word stress on the final vowel'. | Blust 2018 (snippet): ''Melanau' is a dialect chain ... from Balingian in the north to the mouth of the Rejang River in the south, and from there upriver to Kanowit ... In all of these communities for which field data are available stress follows a pattern similar to that of Malay, falling on the penultimate vowel unless that vowel is schwa followed by a single consonant, in which case it shifts rightward to the last syllable.'
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states the rule for Matu, Daro or Belawai themselves. The two chain-level generalisations that would cover them disagree: Clayre (Dalat data, asserted as 'typical Melanau' and built into a pan-dialect orthography) gives final-syllable primary stress in citation forms with secondary stress on the penult; Blust (whose 1971 field data include Matu) gives Malay-like penultimate stress shifting to the final syllable when the penult vowel is schwa + single consonant. Blust 2013:266 partly reconciles them: Sarawak coastal languages 'tend to be oxytone in citation forms, but paroxytone in phrasal context'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Clayre 1972 (Dalat): secondary stress on the penultimate syllable nucleus of polysyllabic words in isolation; when penult /a/ precedes final /a/ both last syllables carry roughly equal (secondary-level) stress (p.51 fn.1). Nothing for Matu/Daro.
new_statements.exceptions: Clayre p.51 fn.1: penult /a/ before final /a/ -> approximately equal stress on last two syllables. Blust 2018: schwa + single consonant in penult -> final stress. Neither stated for Matu/Daro specifically.
new_statements.domain_note: Clayre's rule is explicitly for the phonological word spoken in isolation (citation forms); at phrase level the final syllable of the stressed word carries the pitch movement. Blust 1988/2018 rules are for citation forms of Mukah and, by his generalisation, other field-data communities. Identity caveat: all quoted statements describe Central Melanau (Dalat cent2101 / Mukah) or the chain as a whole, not daro1239.
new_statements.identity_note: No opened source describes stress for daro1239 itself (Matu, Daro, Pulau Bruit, Belawai/Rajang-delta Melanau). The quoted statements belong to other lects: Clayre 1972 describes Dalat Melanau (Central Melanau, cent2101) and only surveyed Matu/Daro/Rajang; Blust 1988 describes Mukah (cent2101, already in the catalog); Blust 2018's rule is stated for the whole Melanau chain (Balingian to Rejang mouth to Kanowit) on the strength of his field data, which include Matu (1971) but do not name it in the sentence. The variety-specific descriptions that do exist (Norfazila & Wan Robiah 2023 = Matu, Kampung Jemoreng; Norfazila 2026 = Daro; Kawi & Dayang Sariah 2018 = Belawai, Rajang delta) are all segment inventories silent on stress. Note Glottolog's daro1239 vs Zaini Oje's split of Kuala Rajang (Rajang, Jerijeh, Belawai, Paloh) from Matu-Daro; Belawai is administratively in Daro district and Rensch groups Matu with Rajang.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian Languages (revised ed.). Asia-Pacific Linguistics Open Access Monographs 8. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: p.266 (sec.4.3.2.10): 'Historically, these languages [of Sarawak] almost certainly had a pattern of primary stress on the penult unless this vowel was schwa. The contemporary languages, however, tend to be oxytone in citation forms, but paroxytone in phrasal context. Stress in Mukah Melanau generally was recorded as penultimate'. Matu Melanau appears only in Table 9.15 (vowel-breaking reflexes) and p.635-636 (-h accretion). No Matu/Daro stress statement.

tone.quote: Tiga belas varian Melanau (VM) Sarawak telah diselidiki, iaitu Bintulu (BT), Balingian (BLGN), Mukah (MKH), Oya (OA), Igan (IGN), Dalat (DLT), Matu (MT), Daro (DO), Medong (MDG), Sungai UD (SG UD), Rajang (RJG), Kanowit (KNWT) dan Tanjong (TJG). Hasil kajian membuktikan bahawa BMLP yang direkonstruksikan ini memiliki 5 fonem vokal, iaitu *i, *u, *o,*, dan *a dan 6 buah diftong, iaitu *-w, *-aw, *-aj, *-ej, *uj, dan *-oj.
tone.translation: Thirteen Melanau variants (VM) of Sarawak were investigated, namely Bintulu (BT), Balingian (BLGN), Mukah (MKH), Oya (OA), Igan (IGN), Dalat (DLT), Matu (MT), Daro (DO), Medong (MDG), Sungai UD (SG UD), Rajang (RJG), Kanowit (KNWT) and Tanjong (TJG). The results prove that the reconstructed Proto-Melanau has 5 vowel phonemes, namely *i, *u, *o, *[schwa] and *a, and 6 diphthongs, namely *-[schwa]w, *-aw, *-aj, *-ej, *uj and *-oj. [the schwa glyph is lost in the PDF text layer; quote copied as extracted]
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Silent on tone and on word prosody generally; a segmental (vowel/diphthong) reconstruction only.

tone.quote: 3.2 Vokal dan Konsonan Bahasa Melanau Rejang Kesemua fonem vokal dan konsonan BMR ada 21 buah, iaitu empat fomen vokal dan 17 fonem konsonan. Dalam kajian ini, pengkaji akan menghuraikan kedudukan fonem vokal dan konsonan BMR di awal, di tengah dan di akhir kata. Pengkaji turut menjelaskan kedudukan urutan vokal dan diftong BMR dalam bahagian ini.

tone.translation: 3.2 Vowels and consonants of Melanau Rejang. The vowel and consonant phonemes of BMR number 21 in all, namely four vowel phonemes and 17 consonant phonemes. In this study, the researcher will describe the position of the BMR vowel and consonant phonemes at the beginning, in the middle and at the end of the word. The researcher also explains the position of BMR vowel sequences and diphthongs in this section. [scope statement: the phonology chapter is segmental only]
tone.summary: A segment-only phonology (4 V, 17 C, syllable patterns, distinctive features) plus loanword rules; no suprasegmental section exists in the TOC and no prosodic remark on the pages read.
